resources.string: Summer savory
Satureja hortensis
Summer savory; garden savory

An annual aromatic herb with a much-branched erect stem, narrow sessile leaves and small white to pink two-lipped flowers in spaced axillary whorls. The tiny dry fruits are nutlets enclosed by the persistent calyx. It is cultivated as a culinary herb; identification here does not imply medicinal use.
Native from southeastern Europe to Kazakhstan and northwestern Iran; now widely cultivated and naturalised.
Erect annual herb, usually 10–50 cm tall, branching freely above.
Opposite, narrow linear leaves with entire margins, borne without a distinct petiole.
Small white or pale pink tubular flowers with a two-lipped corolla, arranged in axillary whorls.
Four tiny dry nutlets develop inside the persistent calyx.
Common sorrel
Rumex acetosa
Common sorrel; garden sorrel

A perennial dock with a basal rosette and arrow-shaped leaves whose backward-pointing basal lobes distinguish many leaves from those of broad-leaved docks. Minute green to reddish flowers form open branched panicles; the fruit is a three-angled achene enclosed by enlarged inner tepals. Leaves contain oxalic acid, so this identification note is not dietary advice.
Temperate Eurasia and northwestern Africa; introduced in parts of North America and elsewhere.
Perennial herb with a basal rosette and one or more slender flowering stems.
Arrow-shaped basal leaf with two backward-pointing basal lobes; upper leaves become narrower.
Tiny green to reddish flowers in loose, branched terminal panicles.
Three-angled achene enclosed by persistent enlarged inner tepals.
Spinach
Spinacia oleracea
Spinach; garden spinach

An annual crop in the amaranth family, grown for its basal leaves. Plants commonly bear male and female flowers on separate individuals; the inconspicuous green flowers lack showy petals. Female flowers develop into dry fruits with characteristic bristly or horned bracteoles. Spinach leaves contain oxalates; this sheet is for identification, not personalised dietary guidance.
Originating in southwestern Asia and cultivated worldwide as a leaf vegetable.
Annual leafy herb, often forming a low rosette before producing a flowering stem.
Variable simple leaves, often triangular or arrow-shaped, with long petioles in basal growth.
Small green, petal-less flowers; male flowers are clustered and female flowers sit among bracteoles.
Dry seed-like fruit enclosed by persistent bracteoles that may bear two horns.
Red bog-moss
Sphagnum capillifolium
Red bog-moss; acute-leaved bog-moss

A peat-forming moss that makes compact, rounded hummocks, often with red or wine-coloured shoots. Each shoot ends in a dense capitulum surrounded by short spreading and pendent branches. Like other Sphagnum mosses it has no true roots, flowers or seeds; spores form in capsules. Field colour alone cannot reliably distinguish it from similar species such as S. rubellum.
Widespread in northern temperate and boreal regions, especially on acidic peat in oceanic districts.
Low moss forming a dense convex hummock of closely packed shoots.
Tiny leaves on the stem and branches; species identification also uses microscopic cell and leaf characters.
Mosses have no flowers; the upper shoot forms a compact capitulum.
Spores mature in small capsules on specialised stalked shoots.
Iturup strawberry
Fragaria iturupensis
Iturup strawberry; Kuril strawberry

A low perennial wild strawberry from the Kuril Islands, with trifoliolate toothed leaves, runners and white five-petalled flowers. Its red strawberry-like aggregate fruit is formed from numerous tiny achenes on an enlarged receptacle. Published reports differ on its chromosome number; no ploidy claim is made here.
Native to Iturup Island in the southern Kurils; cultivated accessions are held in germplasm collections.
Low perennial herb producing basal crowns and creeping stolons.
Leaves are palmately trifoliolate, each leaflet toothed and softly hairy.
White flower with five petals and a central cluster of numerous stamens and carpels.
Red aggregate accessory fruit with many small achenes embedded across its surface.
Wight’s sago palm
Arenga wightii
Wight’s sago palm; Wight’s arenga

A palm native to the wet forests of southern India, with a stout trunk and large pinnate fronds whose leaflets contrast in colour between the upper and lower surfaces. Branched inflorescences arise from the trunk and develop dark fruits. The fruits contain irritant calcium oxalate crystals and must not be treated as food.
Endemic to the Western Ghats of southwestern India, in humid tropical forest.
Solitary palm with a stout trunk and a crown of long arching pinnate fronds.
Pinnate frond with numerous narrow leaflets, paler or glaucous beneath.
Branched inflorescences emerge successively from the trunk; male and female flowers occur on the same palm.
Clustered rounded fruits darken as they mature; their flesh is irritating because of calcium oxalate.
Skinner’s bromeliad
Androlepis skinneri
Skinner’s bromeliad; Androlepis

A large epiphytic bromeliad of humid lowland forests from southern Mexico to Central America. Its funnel-shaped rosette has long arching, sharply serrate leaves; the branched inflorescence bears conspicuous red bracts and pale flowers, followed by berries. The illustration shows the plant attached to a host branch; the branch is not part of the species.
Southern Mexico through Belize and Central America to Nicaragua, in very humid lowland forest.
Large epiphytic rosette growing on tree branches, with a central branched flowering stalk.
Long arching strap leaves with sharp marginal teeth and a water-holding central funnel.
Branched inflorescence with red bracts and small pale flowers.
Small berries develop within the persistent floral parts.
Clove tree
Syzygium aromaticum
Clove; clove tree

An evergreen tree native to the Maluku Islands. Its opposite glossy leaves have visible oil glands. The familiar spice is the aromatic unopened flower bud: a long hypanthium topped by four sepals and a small unopened corolla. Open flowers are pale with numerous stamens; the later fruit is a dark berry. The plate separates these developmental details from the flowering canopy.
Native to the Maluku Islands of Indonesia; cultivated across tropical regions.
Evergreen small to medium tree with a dense crown and aromatic foliage.
Opposite, simple, elliptic leaves with translucent aromatic oil glands.
Clusters of pale flowers; the unopened pink-red bud is harvested as the clove spice.
Mature flower develops into an oblong dark berry with a persistent calyx.
Biting stonecrop
Sedum acre
Biting stonecrop; goldmoss stonecrop

A very low succulent perennial forming mats on dry, shallow soils and rock. Short creeping shoots carry tightly packed pointed leaves; upright flowering tips bear bright yellow star-shaped flowers. The dry fruits split into several follicles. The common name refers to its sharp taste; do not use wild plants as food or medicine based on appearance.
Native from Greenland and Europe through the Mediterranean region to the Caucasus; introduced elsewhere.
Tiny mat-forming succulent with creeping shoots and short upright flowering stems.
Fleshy pointed leaves densely overlap along the creeping stems.
Bright yellow flower with five pointed petals and ten stamens.
Several dry follicles develop from the flower and release minute seeds.
Teak
Tectona grandis
Teak; Indian teak

A large deciduous tropical tree of the mint family, cultivated widely for durable timber. Its huge opposite leaves are rough above and densely star-haired beneath. Large terminal panicles carry small white flowers; the fruit is enclosed by an inflated papery calyx. The tree is illustrated at reduced leaf scale so its canopy proportions remain credible.
Native from India to Indochina; planted extensively throughout the tropics.
Large deciduous forest tree with a broad crown and scaly bark.
Very large opposite elliptic leaves, rough above and pale with stellate hairs beneath.
Many small white regular flowers in a large terminal panicle.
Rounded fruit enclosed by an inflated, bladder-like persistent calyx.
Volvox carteri
Volvox carteri
Volvox carteri; colonial green alga

A freshwater colonial green alga, not a vascular plant. Its motile spheroid is a hollow gelatinous colony with biflagellate somatic cells at the surface and larger reproductive cells; daughter colonies develop inside the parent before release. The plate enlarges cells and colonies for study and does not imply their true shared scale.
Freshwater habitats; studied globally in laboratory culture as a model volvocine alga.
Free-swimming hollow spherical colony of differentiated cells.
No leaves: the colony surface consists of many small biflagellate cells.
No flowers: reproduction involves specialised cells and formation of daughter colonies.
No fruit or seed; internal daughter spheroids are released from the parent colony.
Chlamydomonas reinhardtii
Chlamydomonas reinhardtii
Chlamydomonas reinhardtii; unicellular green alga

A unicellular freshwater green alga widely used in cell biology. Each motile oval cell has two anterior flagella, a large cup-shaped chloroplast, a pyrenoid and a red eyespot involved in light responses. It has no leaves, flowers, roots or fruits; the magnified details are cellular structures.
Freshwater and moist terrestrial habitats; maintained widely in laboratory cultures.
Microscopic single-celled motile alga, shown as an enlarged field of cells.
No leaves; the cell contains a cup-shaped chloroplast around much of its interior.
No flowers; two anterior flagella propel the cell, and an eyespot senses light.
No fruit or seed; the pyrenoid lies within the chloroplast.
Marimo alga
Aegagropila linnaei
Marimo; lake-ball alga

A filamentous freshwater green alga with several growth forms: attached to substrates, free-floating as filaments or mats, and aggregated into rounded marimo lake balls in particular sheltered lake conditions. It has no roots, leaves, flowers or seeds. The round form is a mass of algal filaments, not a single spherical cell.
A broad but patchy northern-temperate distribution; lake-ball populations occur only under specialised conditions.
Filamentous freshwater alga, here shown as a loose spherical aggregation and a free filament tuft.
No leaves; the body consists of branched green filaments made of serial cells.
No flowers; the illustration details filament branching and cell walls.
No fruit or seed; attached forms can produce rhizoid-like holdfasts.
Costa Rican dragon-fruit cactus
Selenicereus costaricensis
Hylocereus costaricensis (tree name; synonym); red-fleshed dragon-fruit cactus

A climbing cactus with long three-ribbed stems, aerial roots and large night-blooming white flowers. Its red fruit has red pulp with numerous black seeds. POWO accepts Selenicereus costaricensis and treats Hylocereus costaricensis as a synonym; the tree’s name is retained for the exact link.
Native from Nicaragua through Central America to northern Peru; cultivated in tropical regions.
Climbing epiphytic or scrambling cactus with long three-angled stems and aerial roots.
No persistent ordinary leaves; green ribbed stems photosynthesise and bear small spines at areoles.
Very large white funnel-shaped flower that opens at night.
Oblong red-skinned berry with red pulp and many tiny black seeds.
Ariocarpus de Nuevo León
Ariocarpus scaphirostrus
Ariocarpus scaphirostrus; Nuevo León living-rock cactus

A highly localised geophytic cactus from Nuevo León, Mexico. Its solitary, nearly ground-level body has spirally arranged boat-shaped tubercles and lacks the conspicuous spine clusters typical of many cacti; a magenta flower emerges from the woolly centre. It is threatened by its restricted range and collection pressure; the illustration is not a guide to wild collecting.
Known from northeastern Mexico, particularly limestone habitats in Nuevo León.
Solitary low geophytic cactus partly embedded in rocky soil, with a flattened rosette.
True leaves are absent; broad triangular tubercles form the visible spiral body.
Large pink to magenta flower arises from the woolly central areoles.
Small fleshy fruit remains partly concealed among the central wool.
Cactus colonnaire des Andes
Echinopsis macrogona
Echinopsis macrogona; Trichocereus macrogonus (synonym)

A tall columnar cactus accepted by POWO as Echinopsis macrogona; some cactus treatments use Trichocereus macrogonus. Its ribbed green stems bear spine clusters at areoles and large white funnel flowers. The illustration follows the POWO name and does not imply any use of the plant.
Native to western and southern Peru and Bolivia, in dry scrub and desert environments.
Tall branching or clumping columnar cactus with upright ribbed stems.
Leaves are absent; ribs carry areoles with clusters of spines.
Large white funnel-shaped flower borne laterally on a mature column.
Fleshy greenish fruit develops after flowering.
Scille de Morris
Scilla morrisii
Scille de Morris; Othocallis morrisii (synonyme)

An endangered bulbous perennial endemic to the Troodos Mountains of Cyprus. Narrow basal leaves accompany a raceme of blue-violet flowers with six tepals and dark anthers. The plant retreats to an underground bulb outside its growing season; exact flowering timing varies with elevation and weather.
Endemic to the Troodos Mountains of Cyprus, in a very restricted range.
Small bulbous geophyte producing a few basal leaves and an upright flower stalk.
Narrow, strap-shaped leaves arise from the bulb near ground level.
Raceme of blue-violet, six-tepalled flowers with conspicuous dark anthers.
Dry capsule follows flowering; the bulb is the persistent underground storage organ.
Héliamphore de Chimantá
Heliamphora chimantensis
Héliamphore de Chimantá; Chimantá marsh pitcher plant

A perennial pitcher plant described from the Chimantá massif of Venezuela. Its upright tubular leaves form dense clumps on nutrient-poor tepui landscapes; each pitcher has an open mouth and a small nectar spoon rather than a hinged lid. A separate scape bears a small flower. It is not a Nepenthes and its traps are modified leaves.
Endemic to the Chimantá massif in Bolívar, Venezuela, on high tepui habitats.
Clump-forming terrestrial carnivorous herb with many upright pitcher leaves.
Leaves are open tubular pitchers with a nectar spoon at the rim; they collect rainwater and prey.
Small pale flower on a distinct slender flowering scape above the pitchers.
Dry capsule follows flowering; no berry-like fruit is produced.
Rusty bog-moss
Sphagnum fuscum
Rusty bog-moss; rusty peat moss

A compact bog-moss forming dense, firm hummocks, often rusty brown. Its small crowded shoots and rounded capitula differ in habit from long, flaccid aquatic Sphagnum species. Reliable identification may require stem and branch leaves under a microscope, especially because S. fuscum has been confused with S. beothuk in older records.
Circumboreal and northern-temperate peatlands; local abundance and records vary by region.
Dense, low, convex hummock with tightly packed brown shoots.
Very small stem and branch leaves; microscopic characters are needed for confident separation.
Mosses have no flowers; compact terminal capitula contain the young shoot tips.
Spores form in capsules on specialised shoots.
Feathery bog-moss
Sphagnum cuspidatum
Feathery bog-moss; long-leaved floating bog-moss

A pale, soft Sphagnum of bog pools and wet ditches, often growing submerged or floating with long flaccid shoots and unusually long narrow branch leaves. Terrestrial forms can resemble S. fallax, so leaf and branch characters matter. As a moss it has no true roots, flowers or seeds.
Widespread in northern regions, especially bog pools, wet ditches and other acidic wetlands.
Loose, soft aquatic or semi-aquatic moss with long trailing shoots.
Long, narrow branch leaves form a feathery surface; microscopic characters assist identification.
Mosses have no flowers; the shoot tip forms a small capitulum.
Spores develop in capsules on specialised shoots.
Myrtle family
Mostly woody aromatic flowering plants with oil glands and flowers often bearing numerous stamens.
Myrtle family; eucalyptus family
Peat-moss family
Mosses of wet acidic habitats, with capitula and specialised water-holding cells; the family includes Sphagnum.
Peat-moss family; Sphagnum family
Volvocaceae
Freshwater volvocine green algae forming motile colonies of flagellated cells, including Volvox.
Volvox family; colonial green algae
Chlamydomonadaceae
Mostly unicellular green algae, commonly motile by two anterior flagella.
Chlamydomonas family; green algae
Cladophoraceae
Filamentous green algae, many with branched filaments and freshwater or marine growth forms.
Cladophora family; filamentous green algae
